Life from age 4 to 16

I like knowing why an exercise is there. I do not always like doing it after I know why. Apparently those are separate things. I am not making a plan to play forever. Right now I want a season where I get to be on the court. People ask what else I am about and I feel like I have to invent something bigger than the stuff I already do.

  • family: Lives with both parents and a younger sister; aunt and uncle nearby are involved in everyday life.
  • finances: Stable middle-income household; parents plan purchases carefully and support one travel sport.
  • geography: Fort Worth, Texas; family visits relatives in east Texas.
  • cultureLanguages: English-speaking Black family; basketball, cookouts, and church gatherings connect several generations.
  • school: Public high school; school basketball player with solid practical math performance.
  • accessOpportunities: Coaches, supervised injury rehabilitation, a recreation center, home internet, and occasional access to an uncle’s delivery-route planning.
  • Age 4–5

    Darius loved chasing bubbles and repeatedly climbing the same playground ladder. His sister was too small to join, so he assigned her the job of cheering from a blanket. His parents remember an energetic child, but he also spent long rainy mornings sorting sports cards with his uncle and arguing about made-up teams.

  • Age 6–7

    At six he joined a recreation basketball group because his best friend was there. He liked passing drills and hated waiting for games to begin. Losing could ruin the ride home. His mother eventually stopped analyzing each game with him, and their trips became easier when they talked about dinner instead.

  • Age 8–9

    At eight he began asking why muscles felt sore after running. A children’s body book supplied explanations he partly understood and repeated too confidently. He liked testing how far he could jump, then forgot to record most measurements. His interest was in moving and comparing, not in keeping a careful research notebook.

  • Age 10–11

    At ten he rode with his uncle during an approved daytime delivery outing. He enjoyed checking stop order and matching parcels to a printed list. The route changed after a closure, which seemed like a puzzle. He was less interested in the customer conversations and mostly wanted to see whether they could recover the lost time.

  • Age 12–13

    At twelve basketball became more serious. Video clips made him compare his body with older players, and he started taking criticism personally. A coach helped him focus on one controllable part of practice. He improved his foot placement through repetition, although he still disliked being corrected in front of teammates.

  • Age 14–15

    At fourteen a sprained ankle interrupted his season. Qualified adults directed treatment and rehabilitation; Darius tracked the assigned exercises and asked why particular movements were limited. He liked understanding recovery but hated the slow pace. He sometimes skipped the last set, then admitted this when asked instead of pretending the plan had failed.

  • Age 16

    At sixteen he is playing again and wants to finish a full healthy season while keeping his grades steady. He enjoys explaining a familiar warm-up to younger players with a coach present. He also helps plan family errands efficiently. He is curious about bodies and transport systems without assuming those interests belong together.

Life now

  • enjoys: Basketball movement · Understanding recovery exercises · Planning efficient errand routes
  • avoids: Public correction · Slow repetitive recovery work when impatient
  • activities: School basketball · Coach-supervised younger-player warm-ups · Family errand planning
  • demonstratedSkills: Adjusts practiced foot placement · Matches stops to a list · Explains a familiar movement clearly
  • unfamiliarActivities: Clinical assessment · Advanced anatomy · Running a delivery operation
  • motivations: Reliable participation · Seeing the reason behind instructions
  • ambitions: Complete a healthy school season · Maintain grades while playing
  • struggles: Comparison with online athletes · Impatience with gradual progress · Difficulty receiving visible correction
  • supports: Coach · Parents who reduce performance pressure · Rehabilitation professionals when needed
  • practicalConstraints: Sports schedule · One travel sport budget · Access to specialized body knowledge mostly through school or treatment

Still uncertain: Would interest in body mechanics continue outside sport and personal recovery? · Does route planning stay enjoyable when customer demands enter the problem?

He is unsure about slow ongoing therapy work and has no clinical assessment experience. The offered physician, nursing, and dental role questions do not describe the rehabilitation exploration he wants, so their selections stay empty.

Career: Occupational Therapists

Preparation: Texas occupational therapist license.

  • Accredited entry-level OT master’s or doctorate.
  • Complete fieldwork and pass NBCOT.
  • Pass Texas law exam and complete fingerprinting.

Annual pay before tax: $84,505 · TWC entry-wage proxy · entry

Budget result: This pay covers your lifestyle. Your costs and savings fit, with money left over.

Financial assumptions: A healthy season and maintaining grades are current wishes, not an adult budget plan. Recreation index 2 allows continued basketball or fitness as a plausible continuation, not a premium sport assumption. A small rental, reliable used car, ordinary groceries, weekly casual meal, modest getaway, occasional entertainment, basic clothes, and growing savings are single-adult reference choices.
